lessons.title: No HRA in Your Salary? Claiming Rent Under Section 80GG

body.text: If your pay has no HRA, the tax law has not forgotten you. Section 134 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 80GG of the 1961 Act) gives a rent deduction to freelancers, business owners and employees without HRA. But its cap is ₹60,000 a year, so it is a consolation prize, not a substitute for HRA.

children.text: India has millions of renters who never see an HRA line: freelance designers and developers, independent consultants, doctors and chartered accountants in practice, small business owners, and employees of startups whose CTC is one lump of basic plus special allowance. Lesson 2 told them the HRA exemption was not available. This lesson covers what they can claim instead.

markDefs.definition: A deduction from total income for rent paid on your own residence, available under the old regime to people who have no HRA exemption and do not own a home where they live or work. It replaced Section 80GG of the 1961 Act.

children.text: is open to anyone paying rent for their own home, salaried or self-employed, who meets these conditions for the tax year.

cells: You have no HRA exemption under Schedule III (Table: S. No. 11)
Your salary has no HRA component, or you have no salary at all. If you receive HRA, use the HRA exemption instead
You pay rent for accommodation you occupy as your own residence
Furnished or unfurnished, it must be the home you actually live in
Neither you, your spouse, your minor child nor your HUF owns a residential home where you ordinarily live, work or run your business
A flat owned by your spouse in the same city rules you out
If you own a home elsewhere, you do not claim it as self-occupied
A let-out flat in another city is fine. A hometown flat you treat as self-occupied blocks the deduction
You are on the old tax regime
Section 134 is not available under the new regime
You file the declaration in Form 31
Form 31 replaced Form 10BA and is filed on the e-filing portal before your return

body.title: Quick Check: Who Qualifies?
body.question: Which of these people can claim the Section 134 rent deduction, assuming all are on the old regime and pay rent where they live?
options: Rhea, a salaried analyst in Chennai whose payslip shows HRA of ₹20,000 a month
Imran, a freelance video editor in Mumbai who owns a flat in Nashik that he has let out
Pooja, a doctor with her own clinic in Indore, whose husband owns a flat in Indore
Siddharth, a consultant in Delhi who owns a flat in Dehradun he treats as self-occupied
body.explanation: Imran has no HRA and owns no home in Mumbai, and his Nashik flat is let out, not claimed as self-occupied. Rhea receives HRA, so she should use the HRA exemption. Pooja is blocked because her spouse owns a home in the city where she lives and works. Siddharth is blocked because he claims his Dehradun flat as self-occupied.

markDefs.definition: For Section 134, your total income for the tax year before allowing this deduction, which means after your other deductions such as Section 123 (80C).

body.label: Maximum Section 134 deduction
body.context: Unchanged at ₹5,000 a month. For most renters in large cities, this cap is the limit that binds.

body.text: Under the old Section 80GG, "adjusted total income" excluded certain income such as long-term capital gains and short-term capital gains taxed at special rates. Section 134 refers to total income before this deduction, and commentators differ on whether those exclusions still apply. If you have significant capital gains, check the current position with a chartered accountant before calculating the 10% and 25% limits.

children.text: Ananya is a freelance UX designer in Andheri, Mumbai. Her taxable professional income is ₹12,00,000 and she invests ₹1,50,000 under Section 123 (80C), so her total income before Section 134 is ₹10,50,000. She pays ₹35,000 a month in rent.

Her total income falls to ₹9,90,000 and her tax from ₹1,32,600 to ₹1,14,920, a saving of ₹17,680. Because the deduction pulls ₹50,000 of her income below the ₹10 lakh line, part of it is saved at 30% and part at 20%. On ₹4,20,000 of rent a year, that is a relief of about 4%.
HRA vs Section 134: Why Your Salary Structure Matters

For salaried employees, the gap between the two routes is huge. Take two employees in Bengaluru, each with ₹12,00,000 gross salary and ₹35,000 a month rent, both on the old regime with ₹1,50,000 of 80C. The only difference is that one has ₹30,000 a month of HRA on a ₹60,000 basic, while the other has the same pay as basic plus special allowance.

body.title: Rent relief on ₹35,000 a month in Bengaluru
Scenario: The Startup Offer Letter
body.scenario: Karthik is joining a Bengaluru startup at ₹12,00,000 CTC. The offer letter shows basic ₹60,000 a month and special allowance ₹40,000 a month, with no HRA. He will pay ₹35,000 a month rent, plans to use the old regime and is in the 30% slab. HR says the structure is "flexible before joining".
body.prompt: Should Karthik ask for part of his special allowance to be paid as HRA? What is it worth?
body.modelAnswer: Yes. If ₹30,000 of the special allowance is reclassified as HRA, his gross pay is unchanged, but his rent relief moves from the Section 134 deduction of ₹60,000 to an HRA exemption of ₹3,48,000. That removes an extra ₹2,88,000 from his taxable income, worth about ₹89,856 a year at 30% plus cess. It costs the employer nothing, since HRA and special allowance are both just salary to them. He should still check the Labour Code rule that allowances cannot exceed 50% of total remuneration, which HR will handle, and compare old and new regime tax before deciding on the old regime.

children.text: When a Small Deduction Makes a Big Difference

The deduction is modest, but at the old regime's ₹5 lakh rebate line it can be decisive. Farida tutors students from her rented flat in Aliganj, Lucknow. Her total income is ₹5,20,000 and she pays ₹7,000 a month in rent.

A ₹32,000 deduction wipes out ₹17,160 of tax, because it takes her total income below ₹5 lakh, where the old regime rebate cancels the tax entirely. Always check where a deduction lands you, not just its size.

body.text: Compare regimes before claiming. Farida's total income of ₹5,20,000 would attract no tax under the new regime either, thanks to its ₹12 lakh rebate. The Section 134 deduction matters most for people who are firmly better off in the old regime for other reasons.

body.title: Try It: Rakesh in Jaipur
body.prompt: Rakesh is a chartered accountant in practice in Jaipur with total income of ₹9,00,000 before the Section 134 deduction. He pays ₹12,000 a month rent, owns no home, receives no HRA and is on the old regime. What is his Section 134 deduction? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: Limit 1: ₹1,44,000 minus 10% of ₹9,00,000 (₹90,000) = ₹54,000. Limit 2: 25% of ₹9,00,000 = ₹2,25,000. Limit 3: ₹60,000. The smallest is Limit 1, so his deduction is ₹54,000, just below the cap because his rent is modest relative to his income.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Declaration
body.textWithBlank: To claim the Section 134 rent deduction, you must file a declaration on the e-filing portal in Form ___, which replaced Form 10BA.
body.explanation: Form 31 under the Income-tax Rules, 2026 records your rent details and confirms you meet the conditions, including that you and your family do not own a home where you live or work. File it before your return.

body.title: Claiming Section 134 Step by Step
steps: Confirm your salary has no HRA component, or that you have no salary
Confirm that you, your spouse, your minor children and your HUF own no home in the city where you live or work
If you own a home elsewhere, confirm you are not claiming it as self-occupied
Calculate total income before the deduction, after your other deductions, then work out the three limits
File Form 31 on the e-filing portal with your rent and landlord details, before filing your return
Claim the deduction in your return under the old regime, and keep the rent agreement and bank records of rent paid

cards.definition: The Income-tax Act, 2025 rent deduction for people without HRA exemption. Replaced Section 80GG. Old regime only.
The smallest of rent minus 10% of total income, 25% of total income, and ₹5,000 a month (₹60,000 a year).
Total income before this deduction, after other deductions. Whether special-rate capital gains are excluded, as under 80GG, should be checked.
The declaration for the Section 134 deduction under the Income-tax Rules, 2026, filed on the e-filing portal. Replaced Form 10BA.
No deduction if you, your spouse, minor child or HUF own a home where you ordinarily live or work, or if you claim a home elsewhere as self-occupied.

points: Section 134 (formerly 80GG) gives a rent deduction to freelancers, business owners and employees without HRA, under the old regime only
The deduction is the smallest of rent minus 10% of total income, 25% of total income, and ₹60,000 a year
You are blocked if you, your spouse, minor child or HUF own a home where you live or work, or if you claim another home as self-occupied
File the declaration in Form 31 before your return
For salaried employees, an HRA component is worth far more than Section 134, so ask for HRA in your salary structure if you rent
A small deduction can still be decisive near the ₹5 lakh old regime rebate line, but always compare with the new regime first

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax, legal or financial advice. It reflects Section 134 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 and the Income-tax Rules, 2026 as understood at the time of writing. The treatment of certain income in the total income calculation may be clarified further. Verify current rules or consult a qualified chartered accountant before acting.
